explanation:
## Cold vs Hot Wallet

A **cold wallet** keeps your private keys offline — a hardware device (Ledger, Trezor, Keystone) or a paper/metal seed backup. Because the keys never touch an internet-connected machine, remote hacks, malware, and phishing drains can't reach them. The trade-off is friction: you have to physically confirm transactions.

A **hot wallet** keeps keys on an online device — a browser extension or mobile app like MetaMask, Phantom, or Trust Wallet. It's instant and convenient for swaps, payments, and dApps, but anything connected to the internet is exposed to a much larger attack surface.

## The 80/20 Rule

The widely cited security guideline is to keep the bulk of your holdings in cold storage and only an everyday "spending" amount hot. A common split is **80% cold / 20% hot**, adjusted by how often you actually transact: the more you trade or use dApps, the more you keep hot (within reason); the more it's a long-term hold, the more goes cold.

This calculator turns that principle into specific dollar amounts from your total holdings and usage frequency (1–10).

## Suggested Allocation by Holding Size

| Total holdings (USD) | Cold storage | Hot wallet | Recommended setup |
|---|---|---|---|
| Under $500 | 60–70% | 30–40% | Reputable hot wallet may suffice; hardware optional |
| $500 – $5,000 | ~80% | ~20% | Entry hardware wallet (Ledger Nano / Trezor) |
| $5,000 – $50,000 | 85–90% | 10–15% | Hardware wallet + small hot wallet for activity |
| Over $50,000 | 90%+ | <10% | Hardware wallet + consider multisig (2-of-3) |

Percentages are a starting point, not a rule. A frequent trader may justify a larger hot slice; a buy-and-hold investor should skew even colder.

## Security Essentials

- **Never store your seed phrase digitally** — no photos, no cloud notes, no password managers. Write it on paper or stamp it on metal, stored offline in more than one location.
- **Not your keys, not your coins.** Coins left on an exchange are controlled by the exchange; a hack or freeze puts them at risk.
- **Verify the receiving address** on the hardware device screen, not just the computer — clipboard-hijacking malware swaps addresses.
- **Use multisig for large holdings** so no single compromised key can move funds.

This tool is for educational reference only and is not financial or security advice.

faq.a: An offline hardware wallet (like Ledger or Trezor) that stores crypto securely. Maximum security for long-term holdings.
A software-based online wallet (such as MetaMask or Trust Wallet). Convenient for frequent transactions and everyday use.
Keep 80% of your crypto in cold storage for safety and 20% in a hot wallet for convenient access and trading.

faq.q: Why shouldn't I keep my crypto on an exchange?
faq.a: On an exchange, you don't own your private keys. As the saying goes: 'Not your keys, not your coins.'

faq.q: How do I securely back up my wallet seed?
faq.a: Write your seed phrase on paper or engrave it on metal, then store it offline in multiple safe locations. Never photograph or store it digitally.
A wallet that requires multiple signatures (like 2-of-3 keys) to approve transactions. More secure for larger holdings.

faq.q: How much does a hardware wallet cost?
faq.a: Ledger Nano: $80-150. Trezor: $70-250. A one-time investment for decades of security.

faq.q: Should I keep different cryptocurrencies in different wallets?
faq.a: It can help. Many people keep long-term holds (like Bitcoin or ETH) in cold storage and keep only the tokens they actively trade or stake in a hot wallet. Separating a high-value 'savings' wallet from a 'spending' wallet limits how much is ever exposed in a single compromise, and makes it easier to apply stricter security (like multisig) only where it matters.
